item.title: Regularized Score Centering
item.description:
Institution: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign | Authors: Hao Bai, Chenlu Ye, Xuanchang Zhang, Aviral Kumar, Tong Zhang

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

item.title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement
item.description:
Authors: Xin Yu, Fei Xia, Jiaqi Pan, Youbao Tang, Chengzhi Liu

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract Continual recursive self-improvement lets harness optimizers reuse and revise prior edits across changing benchmarks or policy models by storing rationales, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation contexts in a self-improvement memory, improving final scores over continuation baselines. Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Abstract

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation (p=0.003).

item.title: MPEG-Diffusion: Mixed-Resolution Video Generation
item.description:
Institution: Roblox Corporation | Authors: Dennis314, Dennis Menn, Tianpei Gu, Guande He, a-r-r-o-w

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract MPEG-Diffusion reduces the computational cost of video diffusion transformers by generating only a self-selected high-resolution region with dual-resolution attention and a mixed-resolution decoder, achieving faster denoising without quality loss. Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Abstract

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) generate realistic videos, but their heavy computational cost limits broader real-world applications. Mixed-resolution generation reduces this cost by generating the visually important region at high resolution (HR) and the rest at low resolution (LR), yet existing methods suffer a severe quality drop on videos and require knowing the HR region in advance. We show that these failures are not inherent to mixed resolution, and propose MPEG-Diffusion to address their three root causes: (1) dual-resolution attention to mitigate the curse of mixed resolution, where each query reads the K/V of its own resolution, (2) a mixed-resolution decoder to blend the HR and LR latents before decoding and resolve distortion, and (3) a self-selected HR region using the DiT's knowledge to find the visually important region without requiring it in advance. Processing only 30% of full-resolution tokens, MPEG-Diffusion speeds up denoising by 4.8times on Wan2.1 14B (3.8times on 1.3B), outperforming prior methods on nearly every metric. In the user study, we demonstrate the high quality of MPEG-Diffusion, with raters preferring it over prior mixed-resolution methods in over 90% of pairs and rating it close to full resolution.

item.title: Agentic On-Policy Distillation Implicitly Reshapes LLMs' ReAct Patterns
item.description:
Authors: Deyang Kong, Zhaoyi Li, Sijian Ren, Yuan Wei, Ying Wei

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract On-policy distillation can improve or degrade language-model agent interaction across domains, and selectively retaining teacher-preferred positions mitigates negative transfer at a cost to source-domain learning. Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Abstract

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers specialized capabilities to language-model agents, but its cross-domain effects on interaction remain unclear. We investigate how OPD reshapes ReAct interaction patterns across mathematics, ALFWorld, and τ^2-bench, focusing on reasoning, actions, and observation acquisition. General-reasoning supervision reduces mathematical tool attempts from 70.4% to 14.4% while increasing accuracy from 16.7% to 38.0%; code-interpreter supervision improves household actions and retail queries. In contrast, ALFWorld supervision reduces τ^2-bench accuracy from 41.5% to 6.6%, accompanied by frequent tool calls that violate user-information dependencies. To address negative transfer using only source-domain training trajectories, we explore selective OPD guided by teacher preference changes before and after domain-specific RL. Retaining the top 95% of positions raises τ^2 accuracy from 11.5% to 29.9% with a source-learning trade-off.

item.title: π^4: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
item.description:
Authors: Yifan Wang, Weiguang Zhao, Ni Yang, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract This unified foundation model enables the recovery of dense geometry, camera poses, and object tracking from diverse, uncalibrated observations in 4D scenes using a shared geometry and motion branch architecture. Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Abstract

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash π^4 is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, π^4 achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.

item.title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding
item.description:
Institution: The Chinese University of Hong Kong | Authors: Fan Zhang, Hao Wu, Jinyang Wu, Hongyu Qu, Zheng Lian

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce MedJev, a system one vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, MedJev removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, MedJev-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of 7.93\% and a 6.04times end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that MedJev-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.

Abstract

item.title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
item.description:
Institution: OPTML Group @ MSU | Authors: Chongyu Fan, Gaowen Liu, Ramana Rao Kompella, Jason Corso, Sijia Liu

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract ResWAM combines visual residual learning in frozen DINOv3 features with a lightweight dual-branch DiT trained via conditional flow matching to improve vision-language-action policy success while lowering training and inference compute. Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Abstract

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over π_{0.5}) at 92.7 ms latency.

item.title: Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose
item.description:
Authors: ivanpodd, Ivan Poddiakov, BearSubj13, Ivan Kruzhilov, Galina Zubkova

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract A comprehensive benchmark evaluates time-series classification methods on a large clinical breath dataset under realistic temporal splits, showing that sensor drift lowers performance and recurrent models are most consistent across diseases. Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Abstract

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic benchmarks that compare machine learning methods under realistic conditions, particularly sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode. Most existing studies rely on small, private datasets with inconsistent protocols, rendering results non-comparable and slowing progress. We introduce Breath-Dx, the first comprehensive benchmark of time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening. Our work leverages the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset, the largest public clinical eNose collection to date, comprising 1,234 patients across nine diagnostic groups, each providing a 17-channel multivariate time series with explicit temporal train/test splits that account for sensor drift. We systematically evaluate 10 methods spanning four families: feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based, and time series architectures. All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation (0.05-0.12 AUC drop compared to random cross-validation), confirming that drift embeds a strong temporal signal. Under this realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance. Recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance across diseases, while specialized time series methods achieve the highest peak results. Demographic confounders matter: breath signals provide independent diagnostic value for some conditions but add little beyond age for others. We release the S-OH dataset, all temporal splits, evaluation protocols, and code to enable reproducible research and accelerate progress in clinical breathomics.

item.title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models
item.description:
Institution: Show Lab | Authors: Jack97, Ke Sun, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yike Zhang, Yanzhe Chen

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.

Abstract

item.title: Multi-Branch Transformer
item.description:
Authors: Gaotang Li, Lingjie Chen, Chunyuan Deng, Zhiwei Xu, Hongzheng Chen

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract Branching Transformer blocks into parallel parameterized branches, combined with shared KV caching, improves language model quality and inference efficiency compared with standard sequential Transformers. Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Abstract

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.

item.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
item.description:
Authors: Hyunjong Ok, Jaeho Lee

arXiv Links

arXiv | PDF

AI summary

Abstract When large language models write neural network weights without gradient-based training, they tend to design sparse table or associative-memory models that outperform same-sized Transformers with far fewer parameters and faster GPU inference, though pretrained LLMs remain more accurate. Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Abstract

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
